title: Philidor: the passive defence that works

D0.outcome: Explains the Philidor idea: the defending rook cuts the attacking king off from the pawn, and passivity is correct because the defender waits for the pawn to advance.

D1.outcome: Sets up the defence in the standard position and states the one condition that triggers the switch to checking from behind.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled rook endings, decides between Philidor, active defence and Lucena-avoidance, with the reason.

D3.outcome: Predicts how the wrong rook placement lets the attacker reach a Lucena position.

sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §5 item 25 (the 'passive defence is always wrong' claim has counter-examples such as the Philidor)
conditions: The defending king stands in front of the pawn near the queening square and the defending rook holds the rank the pawn must cross, cutting the attacking king off; verify each skeleton with the tablebase.
contrasts: The rook stands on the wrong rank, allowing the attacker to build the bridge.
Rook endings with the pawn on a rook file, where other drawing methods apply.
